lesson.title: Spotting the Odd One Out: Outliers and the 1.5 IQR Rule
lesson.summary: An outlier is a data value that falls unusually far from the rest of the distribution, and the 1.5 times IQR rule gives a standard, objective way to flag one instead of relying on a gut feeling.
lesson.body:
An outlier is a data value that lies unusually far from the bulk of the rest of a distribution, distant enough that it does not seem to fit the general pattern of the other observations. Outliers matter because they can be the most informative point in a data set, a genuine anomaly worth investigating, or they can be nothing more than a typo or measurement error, and distinguishing between those possibilities is a core skill connected directly to reading the overall shape of a distribution described earlier in this unit.

Rather than relying on a visual guess about what counts as "unusually far," statisticians use a standard rule based on the interquartile range, or IQR, which measures the spread of the middle 50 percent of the data. First, sort the data and find the first quartile, Q1, and third quartile, Q3, then compute IQR as Q3 minus Q1. Any value below Q1 minus 1.5 times the IQR, or above Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR, is flagged as an outlier. These two boundary values are often called the lower and upper fences.

Here is a worked example using nine values: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 45, already sorted. With nine values, the median is the middle one, the fifth value, which is 16. To find Q1, look at the four values below the median, 12, 14, 15, 15, and take the median of that lower half: the average of the middle two, 14 and 15, giving Q1 equal to 14.5. To find Q3, look at the four values above the median, 17, 18, 19, 45, and take the median of that upper half: the average of 18 and 19, giving Q3 equal to 18.5. The IQR is 18.5 minus 14.5, which is 4. The upper fence is Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR: 18.5 plus 1.5 times 4, which is 18.5 plus 6, or 24.5. Since 45 is greater than 24.5, it is flagged as an outlier, while every other value in the data set falls comfortably inside the fences.

The 1.5 times IQR rule connects directly to shape: outliers are exactly what stretch out the tail in a skewed distribution, and a single extreme outlier can sometimes be mistaken for genuine skew, or vice versa. The distinction is that skew describes a gradual, consistent thinning of many points into a tail, while an outlier is typically one or two points sitting apart from that pattern entirely, as the 45 does above, isolated far past the rest of the values rather than gradually trailing off from them.

Once an outlier is identified, the next step is judgment, not just arithmetic: check whether it reflects a real, valid observation, like the very expensive home from the right-skew example earlier, or a data entry mistake that should be corrected or removed. Outliers also matter practically because, as later sections on mean and median show, they can pull the mean substantially while barely affecting the median, which is exactly why resistant measures of center are preferred whenever a distribution contains one or more outliers.
